newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA LOOKS TO MORE TAX SELF-ASSESSMENT.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA LOOKS TO MORE TAX SELF-ASSESSMENT.

text.p: The South African Revenue Services hoped to overcome the backlog of income tax return assessments by accrediting firms to do the assessments for it, chief executive Piet Liebenberg said on Monday.
He said discussions had been held with the South African Institute of Chartered Accountants and other professional bodies about establishing a new organisation of taxation practitioners.

This would accredit firms which met certain standards and which would be able to certify that assessments complied with the law. SARS would retain the right to cross-check these assessments from time to time but the aim was to encourage greater self-asessment.
"This works extremely well in other parts of the world and we know that once this has been put in place...the backlogs will hopefully be wiped out in a matter of months," he said.
This would avoid duplication and take the pressure off SARS to get assessments up to date. The accredited firms would charge their clients for the service.

Asked whether SARS would be able to trust these outside assessors given the culture of tax avoidance in South Africa, Liebenberg said it would soon be able to determine which firms it could trust and which it could not.
Liebenberg said that the planned autonomy of SARS would allow it to offer more competitive market related salaries to attract skilled staff.

"We need to do that because of the skills in the private sector and the various tax schemes that they come up with. We need to be up to par with those skills in order to assess them," Liebenberg said.
But this did not mean that SARS would be a market leader.
"It is not only money that counts. We also have to create an environment in which people want to work," he said.
SARS had lost 1,300 skilled staff who had taken voluntary severance packages and Liebenberg said that staff turnover in SARS over the last year had been close to 30 percent.
"From a managerial point of view this is almost a nightmare," he said.
He was now aiming for turnover of not more than 1 percent a month.

He said the funding of SARS was still being finalised. It would be given a percentage of gross revenue collections but there would be a transitional period during which it would have to operate on the budget provided for it by Finance Minister Trevor Manuel.
This budget was 947 million rand in 1997/98. "(It is) clear that the budget will not be sufficient and we are looking at ways and means how we can overcome this," Liebenberg said.
SARS planned to outsource some of its information processing work, he said.
